q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for this schema. Both return the set of (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs such that: (a) ITEMN exists in ITM and 1 < ITEMN < 20, and (b) there exists at least one ITP row for that ITEMN that joins to a PUR row with ODATE > 85. In Q1, DISTINCT is applied inside the subquery on (ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN) before joining to ITM; in Q2, DISTINCT is applied after joining ITM, ITP, PUR. Because the join to ITM is on the primary key (one row per ITEMN) and all joins are inner joins, moving DISTINCT outside does not change the resulting set of (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema and standard SQL semantics: ITM.ITEMN is a primary key (removing any possibility of row-multiplication from ITM), joins are inner, and both queries ultimately apply DISTINCT over the same (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs after enforcing PUR.ODATE > 85 and the ITEMN range. Thus, any duplicates introduced by ITP/PUR are eliminated in both queries.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Q2 returns all (A,B) from R2 that have a matching A in R1. Because R2 has a primary key on A, the aliases Y and Z refer to the same single R2 row per A. Q1 adds the predicate Y.B = Z.B. In SQL, NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN (not TRUE), so when R2.B is NULL the extra predicate in Q1 filters the row out, while Q2 still returns it. Thus they differ precisely when R2.B is NULL for a matched A.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R1 (A, B) VALUES (1, 10);
INSERT INTO R2 (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Make R1 contain a row with A=1. Make R2 contain the unique row for A=1 with B=NULL. Then Q2 returns (1, NULL) while Q1 returns no row because Y.B = Z.B evaluates to UNKNOWN for NULLs.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent under the given schema. Q1 deduplicates (ITEMNO, NP) in ITP before joining to ITM; Q2 performs the join first and then deduplicates on (NP, TYPE, ITEMNO). Because ITM has a primary key on ITEMNO, the join from ITP to ITM is many-to-one, and TYPE is functionally determined by ITEMNO. Thus DISTINCT before the join on (ITEMNO, NP) yields the same set of (NP, TYPE, ITEMNO) as DISTINCT after the join. NULL-handling and unmatched joins behave identically in both queries.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists given the schema: the primary key on ITM(ITEMNO) ensures at most one ITM row per ITEMNO, so the placement of DISTINCT (before vs. after a many-to-one inner join) does not change the result. Both queries return exactly one row per distinct (ITP.ITEMNO, ITP.NP) with NP > 1000 that has a matching ITM row.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 joins ITM to the set of DISTINCT (ITEMNO, NP) pairs from ITP; Q2 joins ITM to ITP and then applies DISTINCT on (ITEMNO, NP). Because ITM has a primary key on ITEMNO, the join is key-preserving (at most one ITM row per ITEMNO), so applying DISTINCT before or after the join yields the same set of (ITEMNO, NP). Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are equivalent under the given schema, and no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible under the schema. A difference would require the join to duplicate ITM rows (e.g., multiple ITM rows per ITEMNO) or DISTINCT to be on different columns. The primary key on ITM.ITEMNO prevents duplication, both queries project the same two columns, both use an inner join, and NULLs on ITEMNO do not join in either query.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Q1 is a semi-join using IN: it returns each row from ITP whose ITEMN appears in ITL with WKCEN=468 and LOCAN=0. Q2 is an inner join between ITP and ITL with the same predicates, followed by DISTINCT on ITP.* to collapse duplicates caused by multiple matching ITL rows. Because ITP.ITEMN is a PRIMARY KEY (hence unique and NOT NULL), and both queries effectively return one row per matching ITP item, they are equivalent under this schema. NULLs in ITL.ITEMN do not create a difference: they neither match the join (since ITP.ITEMN is non-NULL) nor make IN true for any non-NULL ITEMN when there is no matching non-NULL value.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema and queries. A difference would require duplicates from the join (already removed by DISTINCT), or NULL ITEMN values on the ITP side (disallowed by the PRIMARY KEY), or differing predicates. Therefore, every database instance satisfying the schema yields identical results for Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 returns all team members on projects whose department (in DEPTS) is named 'SECURITY'. Q2 returns only those team members who are on such projects AND whose payroll department (PAYROLL.PDEPT) is also 'SECURITY'. The extra joins in Q2 (via PAYROLL and the equality V1.D = V2.D) enforce that the member’s PAYROLL.PDEPT matches the DEPTS.DNAME, filtering out members assigned to the project but belonging to a different payroll department. Thus, if a team member is on a 'SECURITY' project but their payroll department is not 'SECURITY', Q1 includes them while Q2 excludes them.
counterexample_dsp: Have a DEPTS row with DNAME='SECURITY' and some project P. Put two employees on project P: one with PAYROLL.PDEPT='SECURITY' and one with PAYROLL.PDEPT='OTHER'. Q1 returns both (project-based), while Q2 returns only the one whose payroll department is 'SECURITY' (department-based). Note: the only enforced constraint is TEAMS.TMEMBER must exist in PAYROLL; no constraint forces PAYROLL.PDEPT to match DEPTS.DNAME.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Q1 joins APPLICANT with a single PAYROLL and filters that PAYROLL row by DEPTNO = 29. Q2 self-joins PAYROLL (A and B) on SSNO, filters only the B side by DEPTNO = 29, and then joins to APPLICANT. Because A is unrestricted on DEPTNO and can have multiple rows per SSNO, Q2 can multiply rows (nA * nB) for the same applicant, whereas Q1 only counts matches from a single PAYROLL scan (nX). Thus, when a person has multiple PAYROLL rows with the same SSNO and at least one has DEPTNO = 29, Q2 returns more duplicates than Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Create one applicant with SSNO = 1 and two PAYROLL rows for the same SSNO: one in DEPTNO = 29 and one in a different department. Q1 returns the applicant once (matching the single DEPTNO=29 row). Q2 returns the applicant twice because A can be either PAYROLL row (2 choices) while B contributes the single DEPTNO=29 row (1 choice), producing 2 duplicates.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 uses a tuple IN predicate, which behaves like a semi-join: each qualifying EMP row appears at most once, regardless of how many matching DEPT rows exist. Q2 is an inner join and will duplicate EMP rows when multiple DEPT rows match the same (DEPT, MGR, LOC=3) keys. Thus, under bag semantics, Q2 can return duplicates while Q1 cannot.
counterexample_dsp: Create one EMP row whose (EMP, DEPT) pair matches two identical DEPT rows with LOC=3. Because there are duplicate matching DEPT rows and no uniqueness constraints, Q2 returns the employee twice (once per matching DEPT row), while Q1 returns the employee once.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Step 1. Intent summary: Q1 returns B from R where A=5 and C<1; Q2 returns B from R where A<10. Both are simple selections (no joins/aggregations) and standard 3-valued logic applies to predicates. Divergence: Every row satisfying Q1 (A=5 and C<1) also satisfies Q2 (since 5<10), but Q2 can include additional rows with A<10 that either have A<>5 or have A=5 with C>=1. Therefore Q2 is a strict superset of Q1 in general, so their outputs can differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (5, 100, 0);
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (1, 200, 7);
counterexample_dsp: Add any row with A<10 that does not satisfy (A=5 and C<1). For example, a row with A=1 (any C) or A=5 with C>=1 will appear in Q2 but not Q1. No schema constraints limit this.

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps all users in CITY=3 and left-joins their count of pictures with SIZE > 1,000,000, filling missing counts with 0. Q2 uses an inner join between USER and PICTURE, so users without qualifying pictures are excluded. Therefore, Q1 can return rows (with CNT=0) that Q2 omits. Additionally, Q2’s GROUP BY on (UID, UNAME) can multiply counts if duplicate USER rows exist, while Q1 aggregates pictures only by UID.
counterexample_dsp: Include a user in CITY=3 with no pictures over 1,000,000 bytes (or only smaller ones), and another user in CITY=3 with some large pictures. Q1 will output both users (with CNT=0 for the first), while Q2 will only output the user(s) with large pictures.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. The extra self-join to PIC as W in Q1 does not restrict results because W can be the very same row as V: W.PICUID = X.USRUID and W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE are satisfied by choosing W = V. Since V.PICSIZE >= 500000 already ensures V is a valid picture row, a matching W always exists (the V row itself). With DISTINCT applied in both queries, the result sets are identical.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible under the given schema and predicates. For any (X, U, V) that satisfies Q2, choosing W = V will satisfy Q1, so Q1 cannot exclude any user that Q2 includes, nor include any that Q2 excludes.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Q2 counts shipments per part (GROUP BY Y.PNUM) and joins those counts to PARTS on (PNUM, QOH). Q1 instead checks (PNUM, QOH) IN a subquery that selects Y.PNUM together with COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) but without GROUP BY. In standard SQL this is invalid; in engines that allow it, the subquery returns a single arbitrary Y.PNUM paired with the global COUNT across all matching rows. Hence Q1 compares against at most one (PNUM, total_count) pair, while Q2 matches against many (PNUM, per_part_count) pairs. They differ whenever per-part counts differ from the global count.
counterexample_dsp: Create supplies with SHIPDATE < 10 for two different PNUMs so that the global count is 3, while per-PNUM counts are 2 and 1. Put PARTS rows whose QOH equals the per-PNUM counts (2 for PNUM=1 and 1 for PNUM=2), but no PARTS row with QOH=3. Then Q2 returns both parts (1 and 2), while Q1 compares against a single pair (some PNUM from {1,2}, 3) and returns no rows.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 returns only those EMP rows whose (EMP, DEPT) pair appears in DEPT for rows with LOC = 3 (a semi-join via tuple IN). Q2 returns all EMP rows. They differ whenever an employee’s (EMP, DEPT) does not match any DEPT row with LOC = 3, or when NULLs prevent a match.
counterexample_dsp: Include two EMP rows; only one has a matching (MGR, DEPT) pair in DEPT with LOC = 3. Then Q1 returns a subset (the matching one), while Q2 returns both employees.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 returns the distinct set of A.X values for rows in A that have a matching row in B on A.YA = B.YB. Q2 joins A as X with A as Y on X.X = Y.X (multiplying rows by the number of A-rows sharing the same X) and also requires X.YA = B.YB; it then UNION ALLs an empty result. They can differ because: (1) Q1 includes NULL X values (DISTINCT returns a single NULL), while Q2’s equality join X.X = Y.X filters out rows where X is NULL (NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN). (2) Q1 deduplicates, while Q2 preserves multiplicity due to the self-join.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO B (YB) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO A (X, YA) VALUES (NULL, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Use a row in A with X = NULL and YA matching a row in B. Q1 will output one row with AX = NULL, but Q2 will output no rows because X.X = Y.X is never true for NULL. No constraints prevent NULLs in A.X.

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 filter on different constant string values in the WHERE clause (YX = 'HELLO' vs YX = 'HELLO HI'). With no joins, aggregation, or DISTINCT, the result sets differ whenever the table contains rows matching one literal but not the other.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 10, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 20, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Include at least one row with YX = 'HELLO' and/or one with YX = 'HELLO HI'. This triggers different filtering outcomes: rows with 'HELLO' appear only in Q1; rows with 'HELLO HI' appear only in Q2. No schema constraints restrict this.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Q1 selects distinct value 1 from R1 when there exists a matching R2 row on R1.Y = R2.Y. Q2 does the same join to R2 and additionally self-joins R1 on X.X = Y.X. That extra self-join is redundant: for any qualifying row X in R1, the same physical row can serve as Y (since aliases are independent ranges), so the condition X.X = Y.X is always satisfiable whenever X exists. With DISTINCT on X, both queries return 1 iff there exists at least one R1 row with X=1 whose Y matches some R2.Y. Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for all databases under the given schema, and no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible. The additional self-join in Q2 (R1 Y with X.X = Y.X) does not constrain results beyond Q1, because the X row itself can satisfy the equality. Both queries return {1} exactly when there is some R1 row with X=1 and a matching R2 row on Y; otherwise both return empty.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are logically equivalent. Each requires two equality predicates to be TRUE: Q1 checks A1=A2 and A2=A3; Q2 checks A1=A2 and A1=A3. In SQL, for an equality to be TRUE, both operands must be non-NULL and equal. If both predicates in either query are TRUE, it forces A1, A2, and A3 to be equal and non-NULL, which makes the other query’s predicates TRUE as well. DISTINCT only removes duplicate result rows and does not introduce any difference. Therefore, both queries return exactly the same set of rows for all possible data.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema and standard SQL NULL semantics. The conjunction of equalities in both queries guarantees all three columns are equal and non-NULL, making the predicates equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: No counterexample exists: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Q1 performs a Cartesian product R×R and then selects DISTINCT X.*, which collapses the multiplicities introduced by the join and yields exactly the distinct rows of R. When R is empty, both return empty; when R is non-empty, both return the distinct rows of R.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible to construct under this schema. The cross join in Q1 only multiplies rows but does not filter any X rows; DISTINCT removes duplicates. Since Y is the same base table R with no predicates, it is empty iff R is empty, so Q1 and Q2 always return the same set.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a self-join of R with itself and filters on X.A = Y.A, then selects DISTINCT Y.A. Because SQL equality with NULL is not true, any rows where A is NULL are filtered out. Q2 simply selects DISTINCT A from R, and DISTINCT retains a single NULL value if present. Thus, Q2 can return NULL while Q1 cannot.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Include at least one row where R.A is NULL. Q2 will return a single NULL, whereas Q1 will return no rows because NULL = NULL is not true.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Q1 does a self inner-join on equality of (A1, A2). In SQL, equality with NULL is unknown (not true), so any row where A1 or A2 is NULL will not match—even with itself—and will be eliminated. Q2 simply returns the distinct (A1, A2) pairs from R, and DISTINCT keeps rows with NULLs. Therefore, rows containing NULLs appear in Q2 but are filtered out by Q1.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (NULL, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Include at least one row where A1 or A2 is NULL. Such a row is included by Q2 (DISTINCT over R) but excluded by Q1 (self-join on =, which fails on NULL). No schema constraints prevent NULLs.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are identical except for the table alias (X vs Y). Both compute, for each distinct A, the sum of (A + B) over rows with that A. There are no joins, subqueries, or differing predicates; NULL and aggregation behavior are the same. Therefore, they are equivalent for all possible data and no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: No data condition can trigger a difference; both queries group by A and sum the same expression (A + B) from the same table with only an alias change.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both enforce X > 50 and X < 200; the order of applying WHERE predicates does not change the result. With SQL’s three-valued logic, rows with NULL in X fail both predicates at their respective first filter and are excluded in both queries. No joins, aggregates, DISTINCT, or outer semantics exist that could cause divergence.
counterexample_dsp: No data can make them differ: both compute the intersection (50, 200). NULLs are filtered out identically by the WHERE clauses; duplicates are preserved equally; there are no other constructs that could introduce differences.

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both return exactly the rows of R where X is strictly between 50 and 200. The derived table in Q2 does not change semantics, and there are no joins, aggregates, DISTINCT, or ORDER/LIMIT differences. NULLs are excluded identically by the predicates (three-valued logic) in both queries.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible under the given schema. With a single INT column and simple comparisons X > 50 and X < 200, any row either satisfies both predicates in both queries or is filtered out by both. NULLs are rejected in both queries at the same stage.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 counts all rows in R (COUNT(*) counts every row). Q2 counts only rows where B is not NULL (COUNT(B) ignores NULLs). They differ whenever at least one row has B IS NULL.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (2, 10);
counterexample_dsp: Include at least one row with B = NULL. Then COUNT(*) counts it, but COUNT(B) does not. For example, two rows: one with B = NULL and one with B = 10, so Q1=2 and Q2=1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: No counterexample exists. Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for all instances of R(X INT). For any non-NULL X, (X > 50) OR (X < 200) is always TRUE, so Q1 returns all non-NULL rows and DISTINCT removes duplicates. Q2 takes rows where X > 50 and rows where X < 200, concatenates them (UNION ALL), and then DISTINCT removes duplicates—yielding exactly the distinct set of non-NULL rows. Rows with X = NULL fail both predicates in both queries and are excluded. Thus both queries return the same distinct set of non-NULL X values.
counterexample_dsp: No data can make the results differ. To differ, a row would need to satisfy (X > 50 OR X < 200) without satisfying either X > 50 or X < 200 individually, which is impossible under SQL three-valued logic. NULLs are excluded by both queries; DISTINCT removes all duplicates in both.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10

explanation: Both queries aggregate courses by department after an inner join to DEPARTMENT, returning departments whose total credits exceed 10. They differ only in the COUNT(C.CREDITS) threshold: Q1 requires >5 while Q2 requires >8. Because COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, only non-NULL credit rows are counted. Thus, any department with 6–8 non-NULL credit rows (and SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10) appears in Q1 but not in Q2.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 10, 1000); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 2); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 102, 1, 2); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (3, 103, 1, 2); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (4, 104, 1, 2); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (5, 105, 1, 2); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (6, 106, 1, 2);
counterexample_dsp: Create one department and exactly 6 COURSE rows for it, each with non-NULL credits such that SUM(C.CREDITS) = 12 and COUNT(C.CREDITS) = 6. The inner join includes these rows (since the department exists), the sum condition passes for both queries, the count passes for Q1 (>5) but fails for Q2 (>8).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: Both queries join COURSE→DEPARTMENT→INSTRUCTOR, group by C.DEPT_NAME, and filter groups with MAX(I.SALARY)<75. Q1 keeps groups with SUM(I.SALARY)>100 while Q2 keeps groups with SUM(I.SALARY)>=100. They differ exactly when the sum equals 100 (and max salary <75): Q2 includes the group; Q1 excludes it.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department with exactly one course to avoid duplicate inflation, and two instructors in that department with salaries 50 and 50. Then SUM=100 and MAX=50<75, so Q2 returns the department while Q1 does not.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both join COURSE–DEPARTMENT–TEACHES, group by department, and require SUM(D.BUDGET) > 100000. They differ because Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) in HAVING. When the join produces many duplicate rows with the same department budget (e.g., many TEACHES rows for the same course/department), COUNT counts all duplicates, but COUNT(DISTINCT) collapses them to 1, so Q1 can pass while Q2 fails.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department with a single budget (e.g., 10000), one course in that department, and 11 TEACHES rows for that course. The join yields 11 rows all carrying the same budget. Then SUM(D.BUDGET) = 110000 (>100000). Q1’s COUNT(D.BUDGET) = 11 (>10) passes, but Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) = 1 (not >10) fails.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Both queries group by department and aggregate over the joined rows of COURSE⋈DEPARTMENT⋈TEACHES⋈INSTRUCTOR. They both require AVG(I.SALARY)>50000, but differ in the HAVING condition on the number of distinct salary values: Q1 requires COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4, while Q2 requires COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4. Therefore, any department whose joined rows contain exactly four distinct salary values (with avg>50000) will be returned by Q1 but filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department with one course that has at least one TEACHES row, and exactly four instructors in that department with distinct salaries all above 50000 (e.g., 60000, 70000, 80000, 90000). The join multiplies instructor rows by the (C,T) pairs, but COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY) remains 4 and AVG(I.SALARY) stays >50000, so Q1 returns the department while Q2 returns nothing. No constraints in the provided schema prevent this.

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2
explanation: Both queries join DEPARTMENT to TEACHES on D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4 and then to COURSE on department, group by T.SEMESTER, and return SUM(C.CREDITS) for groups where AVG(C.CREDITS) > 2. They differ only in the HAVING clause: Q1 requires COUNT(D.BUILDING) = 2, while Q2 allows COUNT(D.BUILDING) >= 2. Since COUNT(D.BUILDING) counts non-NULL BUILDING values over the joined rows (including duplicates produced by the joins), any group with at least 3 such rows will be returned by Q2 but filtered out by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Create one TEACHES row with YEAR=2020 and SEMESTER=1. Create three DEPARTMENT rows all with BUDGET=2024 (so all match the TEACHES row) and non-NULL BUILDING. Give each department exactly one COURSE with CREDITS=3. The join produces three rows for semester 1, so COUNT(D.BUILDING)=3 and AVG(C.CREDITS)=3>2. Thus Q2 returns the group (since 3>=2) while Q1 does not (since 3≠2).

q1: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID,DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 groups by (ID, DEPT_NAME) and requires at least two joined rows within the same department per student. Q2 groups only by ID and sums rows across all departments for that student. With NATURAL JOIN, DEPT_NAME is enforced to match across COURSE, DEPARTMENT, and STUDENT, but if the same ID appears in multiple STUDENT rows with different DEPT_NAME values (and the student takes a course in each of those departments), Q2 can count both rows together and return the ID, while Q1 splits them into separate groups of size 1 and returns nothing.
counterexample_dsp: Create two departments (dept 10 and 20) with distinct buildings. Create two courses, one in each department. Insert the same student ID twice in STUDENT, once per department. Have the student take one course from each department, and provide matching SECTION rows (same COURSE_ID/SEC_ID/YEAR and BUILDING equal to the department’s building). Result: the student yields two joined rows with different DEPT_NAME values. Q1 groups by (ID, DEPT_NAME) so each group has count 1 (<2) and returns no row; Q2 groups by ID so total count is 2 (>=2) and returns the ID.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only by DISTINCT in the outer select. Both filter COURSE rows whose CREDITS equals the single value returned by the scalar subquery (max credits among CS courses in departments having more than 2 such courses). If multiple COURSE rows share the same DEPT_NAME and have that CREDITS value, Q2 will return duplicate DEPT_NAMEs while Q1 will deduplicate them. We ensure the subquery is scalar by making only one department satisfy the HAVING clause.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department (e.g., DEPT_NAME=1) that has more than two CS courses with a maximum credit value X (here X=4) so the subquery returns 4. Also ensure there are at least two COURSE rows in that same department with CREDITS=4. Then Q2 returns DEPT_NAME=1 twice, while Q1 returns it once due to DISTINCT. Only one department passes the HAVING so the subquery returns a single value.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in the subquery A: Q1 keeps groups where COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1, while Q2 keeps groups where SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1. This could produce different sets in A (e.g., a single row with TIME_SLOT_ID=2 passes Q2 but not Q1; multiple rows with TIME_SLOT_ID=NULL pass neither; multiple rows with negative/zero can pass Q1 but fail Q2). However, the outer query groups by STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME and applies HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2. Within each group (fixed STUDENT.ID), COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) is at most 1, so the HAVING predicate is always false. Therefore, both Q1 and Q2 always return the empty result set, making them trivially equivalent on all databases.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: the outer HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2 is unsatisfiable when grouping by STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME, so both queries always return no rows regardless of any differences in the subquery A. To observe differences between COUNT vs SUM in A, the outer HAVING would need to be changed (e.g., removed or replaced with HAVING COUNT(*) > 2).

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 groups by (YEAR, COURSE_ID) before filtering, then projects YEAR and sums it per YEAR, effectively counting each qualifying course separately within a year (so the same YEAR can be added multiple times). Q2 groups only by YEAR before filtering, so at most one row per YEAR survives and gets summed once. Thus, when a year has multiple courses each with COUNT(ID) > 4, Q1 multiplies the year value by the number of such courses, while Q2 includes the year only once.
counterexample_dsp: Make one instructor and, in the same year, two different courses each taught in more than 4 rows. Then per-course counts exceed 4 for both courses (Q1 yields two rows for that year, summing to 2*YEAR), while the per-year count also exceeds 4 (Q2 yields one row, summing to YEAR).

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns all courses with their COURSE_ID and TITLE. Q2 returns only those courses where CREDITS > 3. They differ whenever a course has CREDITS <= 3 or CREDITS IS NULL, because such rows appear in Q1 but are filtered out by Q2 (NULL comparisons yield UNKNOWN and are excluded by WHERE).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (101, 1001, 10, 3);
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (102, 1002, 10, 4);

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Step 1. Q1 is an inner equi-join between COURSE and TEACHES filtered to TEACHES.YEAR = 2010; it only returns rows where COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID. Q2 replaces the equality with a non-equi join COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID, which can pair a TEACHES row with many COURSE rows whose COURSE_ID is greater than or equal. DISTINCT just removes duplicates and does not equalize these semantics. Therefore, if there exists a TEACHES row (YEAR=2010) whose COURSE_ID is less than some COURSE.COURSE_ID but has no exact matching COURSE row, Q2 will still return rows while Q1 will not.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 200, 10, 3);
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (10, 1, 1, 2010, 1, 999);
counterexample_dsp: Step 2. Create one COURSE with COURSE_ID = 2 and one TEACHES row for YEAR = 2010 with COURSE_ID = 1. There is no COURSE with COURSE_ID = 1. Q1 finds no match (2 ≠ 1). Q2 matches because 2 >= 1, producing a row. No constraints in the schema prevent this.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation: Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN with a non-equality predicate (INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID). This returns every instructor at least once, and when no TEACHES row has a smaller ID, TEACHES columns are NULL. Q2 uses an INNER JOIN with equality (INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID), returning only rows where IDs match exactly. They differ because of (a) outer vs inner join semantics, and (b) different join predicates (> vs =), so equality matches are excluded by Q1 but included by Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (5, 10, 90000, 1);
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (5, 100, 1, 2024, 1, 5);
counterexample_dsp: Create one instructor with ID = 5 and one TEACHES row also with ID = 5 (and no TEACHES rows with ID < 5). In Q1, the predicate 5 > 5 is false, so the LEFT JOIN yields a row with NULL TEACHES.COURSE_ID. In Q2, the equality join matches and returns the actual COURSE_ID. DISTINCT does not remove this difference.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent and will always return the empty set. In both queries, the subquery S groups by (ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR) and then applies HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > N. Because TIME_SLOT_ID is part of the GROUP BY, each group has at most one distinct TIME_SLOT_ID (1 if TIME_SLOT_ID is non-NULL, otherwise 0). Therefore the HAVING condition (>4 in Q1, >5 in Q2) can never be satisfied. S is always empty, and thus the final NATURAL JOIN with STUDENT (on ID) also returns no rows for both Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: the HAVING clause is unsatisfiable due to grouping including TIME_SLOT_ID. The dataset below illustrates typical data where, despite a student taking many sections with different time slots, both queries still return empty.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 returns departments that offer at least one course with the global maximum number of credits across all courses. Q2 builds a list of each department’s per-department maximum credits, then (due to a join without an ON condition) cross-joins that list with all courses and keeps courses whose credits equal any department’s maximum. Thus Q2 returns departments of courses whose credits match any per-dept max (possibly from another department), not necessarily the global max. Therefore Q2 can include extra departments that Q1 excludes.
counterexample_dsp: Have at least two departments with different per-dept maxima, e.g., dept 10 has a max of 4 and dept 20 has a max of 5 (the global max). Then any course with 4 credits (in any department) will match some per-dept max (4) and appear in Q2, while Q1 only returns departments with courses at the global max (5).
